outputs.L2:
A flexible pipe coupling (200) configured to connect a pressurised main pipe to a service pipe includes:

- an elongated corrugated section (202) extending between a first end (208) and a second end (210) and defining an internal passage. Multiple corrugations are distributed along this section, with each corrugation having a crest (204), at which the passage reaches its largest internal diameter, and a valley (206), at which the passage reaches its smallest internal diameter;
- a first spigot-receiving socket (212) located at the first end of the elongated section; and
- a second spigot-receiving socket (214) located at the second end.

At a specified volumetric flow rate, fluid passing through the corrugated section experiences head loss that does not exceed the head loss through an equal-length, smooth-bore pipe whose internal diameter matches that of the first and second spigot sockets. In addition, the smallest internal diameter of the corrugated passage is larger than the greatest internal diameter of the first and second spigots.
outputs.L3:
The flexible pipe connector is designed to join a pressurised mains pipe to a service pipe. It comprises a longitudinally extending corrugated body that defines an internal bore between first and second ends, with a spigot socket located at each end.

The connector is configured so that, at a defined volumetric flow rate, the head loss through the connector is no greater than the head loss through an equivalent smooth-bored pipe having the same overall length and socket diameter. To achieve this hydraulic performance, the minimum internal diameter of the corrugated bore is greater than the maximum internal diameter of the spigot sockets.
outputs.L4:
A flexible pipe connector is provided for joining a pressurized mains pipe to a service pipe. The connector comprises a flexible, corrugated tubular body having a spigot socket at each end. One socket is configured for connection to the mains pipe, while the other is configured for connection to the service pipe. The sockets may be dimensioned to receive or engage corresponding pipe ends and may incorporate suitable seals or retaining components to form a secure, pressure-tight connection.

Although the corrugations allow the connector to bend and accommodate changes in direction, installation tolerances, ground movement, and relative displacement between the connected pipes, they can also create additional turbulence and flow resistance. To compensate for this effect, the connector has an enlarged minimum internal bore diameter compared with that of an equivalent smooth-bore pipe or conventional connector.

The bore diameter is selected so that the reduction in flow velocity resulting from the increased flow area offsets the hydraulic losses associated with the corrugated internal surface. As a result, the fluid head loss through the flexible connector is no greater than the head loss through an equivalent length of smooth-bore pipe under corresponding flow conditions. The connector therefore provides the mechanical advantages of a flexible, corrugated construction while maintaining the hydraulic performance required for pressurized mains-to-service connections.
outputs.L5:
# A Flexible Pipe

A flexible pipe is designed to transport liquids, gases, or other materials while bending and adapting to movement. Unlike rigid piping, it can be installed around obstacles and used in places where vibration, shifting, or limited space would make conventional pipes unsuitable.

Flexible pipes are commonly made from materials such as plastic, rubber, stainless steel, or layered composites. Their construction depends on the intended application. A lightweight plastic pipe may be suitable for domestic drainage or irrigation, while a reinforced, multi-layer pipe may be required for industrial systems, offshore oil production, or high-pressure gas transport.

One of the main advantages of a flexible pipe is ease of installation. Its ability to bend can reduce the number of joints and fittings needed, saving time and lowering the risk of leaks. It can also absorb vibration, thermal expansion, and ground movement more effectively than many rigid alternatives.

However, selecting the right flexible pipe is essential. Factors such as pressure, temperature, chemical resistance, bend radius, and expected service life must be considered. When correctly specified and maintained, a flexible pipe offers a practical, durable, and versatile solution for a wide range of fluid-transport applications.

counterfactuals.output:
### What is claimed is:

1. **A flexible connector for fluidly coupling a mains pipe to a service pipe, the flexible connector comprising:**  
   an elongate tubular body extending along a longitudinal axis and defining a fluid passage therethrough;  
   a plurality of corrugations formed along at least a portion of the tubular body, the corrugations rendering the tubular body flexible and defining a longitudinally extending corrugated bore;  
   a first spigot-receiving socket disposed at a first end of the tubular body and configured to receive an end portion of the mains pipe; and  
   a second spigot-receiving socket disposed at a second end of the tubular body and configured to receive an end portion of the service pipe,  
   **wherein** at least one internal dimension of the corrugated bore is selected in relation to an internal dimension of at least one of the mains pipe and the service pipe such that an increased flow area provided by the corrugated bore at least partially compensates for frictional head loss caused by the corrugations.

2. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein an effective internal diameter of the corrugated bore is greater than an internal diameter of the service pipe.

3. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein a minimum internal diameter of the corrugated bore is at least equal to an internal diameter of the service pipe.

4. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein a ratio of a hydraulic diameter of the corrugated bore to an internal diameter of the service pipe is selected to provide a predetermined flow rate through the flexible connector at a predetermined pressure differential.

5. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein the corrugated bore has a cross-sectional flow area greater than a cross-sectional flow area of the service pipe by an amount sufficient to offset at least a portion of a pressure loss attributable to the corrugations.

6. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein the plurality of corrugations comprises annular corrugations spaced along the longitudinal axis.

7. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein the first and second spigot-receiving sockets have respective internal diameters corresponding to respective external diameters of the mains pipe and the service pipe.

8. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein each of the first and second spigot-receiving sockets comprises a sealing region configured to form a fluid-tight seal around the respective end portion received therein.

9. The flexible connector of claim 8, wherein each sealing region comprises an annular sealing member retained within an internal groove of the respective spigot-receiving socket.

10. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein the tubular body and the first and second spigot-receiving sockets are integrally formed from a polymeric material.

11. The flexible connector of claim 1, wherein the dimensional relationship between the corrugated bore and the service pipe is selected such that, at a designated flow rate, a pressure drop through the flexible connector does not exceed a predetermined pressure drop through a corresponding length of smooth-bore pipe by more than a specified amount.

12. **A pipe connection assembly comprising:**  
    a mains pipe;  
    a service pipe; and  
    the flexible connector of claim 1, wherein a spigot end of the mains pipe is received in the first spigot-receiving socket and a spigot end of the service pipe is received in the second spigot-receiving socket.

13. The pipe connection assembly of claim 12, wherein the corrugated bore has an effective flow area selected as a function of a corrugation-induced friction factor, a length of the corrugated bore, and an internal flow area of the service pipe.

14. **A flexible pipe connector comprising:**  
    a corrugated tubular portion defining a flow passage and being resiliently deformable to permit angular or lateral displacement between opposite ends thereof;  
    first and second sockets positioned at the opposite ends and configured to receive respective pipe spigots; and  
    **wherein** the flow passage has a hydraulic diameter greater than a hydraulic diameter of at least one of the respective pipe spigots, the difference between the hydraulic diameters being dimensioned to compensate for increased flow resistance produced by an internal corrugated surface of the corrugated tubular portion.
